title: Risk Measures: Volatility, VaR and Drawdown
summary: Three numbers that answer different questions, and each one is silent about exactly the thing you most want to know.

lesson.body:
Three measures dominate risk reporting, and each answers a genuinely different question.

**[[volatility|Volatility]]** — how much returns vary around their average. Symmetric: it treats an unexpected gain exactly like an unexpected loss.

**[[value-at-risk|Value at risk]]** — the loss that will not be exceeded with a stated probability over a stated period. "95% one-day VaR of 1.55%" means a worse day than that is expected one time in twenty.

**[[drawdown|Maximum drawdown]]** — the largest peak-to-trough fall actually experienced. The only one of the three that describes something that happened rather than a distributional property.

**Each is silent about something important.** Volatility says nothing about the shape of the distribution. VaR says nothing about how bad the losses beyond the threshold are. Drawdown says nothing about the probability of a worse one, because it is a single historical realisation.

**So a risk report with one of them is not a risk report.** The three together, plus a stress scenario, is roughly the minimum honest set.

**Value at risk answers "how bad is a bad day?" and refuses to answer "how bad is a catastrophe?"**

A 95% one-day VaR of 1.55% on a 100m portfolio means: on 19 days out of 20, losses should be under 1.55m. It says **nothing whatever** about the twentieth day. The loss then could be 2m or 40m, and the VaR figure is identical in both cases.

Which is why **[[expected-shortfall|expected shortfall]]** exists: the average loss *given* that the threshold was breached. For a [[normal-distribution|normal distribution]] at 95%, expected shortfall is around 1.95% against a VaR of 1.55% — and for a fat-tailed distribution, far higher. It is a strictly better measure and it is less widely quoted, largely because it is less flattering.

Three further limits worth carrying:

**VaR assumes a distribution.** Usually normal, or a historical window. Both understate tails, and the historical version is a claim that the future resembles the sample.

**VaR is not additive across positions in a useful way** — combining two portfolios' VaR figures can produce a number lower than either, which is one reason expected shortfall is preferred technically.

**A VaR limit can be gamed by construction.** Positions with small everyday moves and large rare losses — selling deep out-of-the-money options is the pure case — show low VaR and enormous tail risk. **Any risk limit expressed only in VaR terms is an invitation to sell insurance.**

**Drawdowns are arithmetically asymmetric, and the asymmetry is why they dominate how investing actually feels.**

To recover:

- a **10%** fall needs **+11.1%**
- a **20%** fall needs **+25.0%**
- a **30%** fall needs **+42.9%**
- a **50%** fall needs **+100.0%**
- a **70%** fall needs **+233.3%**

**A 50% loss requires doubling to get back to level.** Volatility, being symmetric, treats the 50% fall and a 50% gain as equally informative. Compounding does not.

Two consequences follow, and the second is the one that decides outcomes.

**Large drawdowns are disproportionately destructive to compound returns**, which is why volatility drag matters and why a strategy with a lower average return and shallower drawdowns can compound to more.

**Drawdowns cause decisions.** A 30% fall triggers redemptions, breaches limits, forces sales and ends careers. **The risk that matters is rarely the risk of a bad outcome — it is the risk of being forced to act at the bottom.** That is a liquidity and governance question, and no distributional measure captures it.

Which is why maximum drawdown, despite being a single unrepeatable observation with no statistical standing, is often the most useful of the three.
A 100m portfolio with 15% annualised volatility, assuming normally distributed returns and 252 trading days.
walkthrough: **Expected shortfall at 95%** — the average loss on the days that exceed VaR — is about **1.95%**, or 1.95m.

**Read that carefully: the 95% VaR says losses stay under 1.55m nineteen days in twenty. It is completely silent about the twentieth, where the average loss is 1.95m and the possible loss is unbounded.**
And the assumption is doing a great deal of work. Real return distributions have fatter tails than the normal, so the true 99% VaR is typically larger than 2.20m — sometimes substantially.

Sanity check worth reusing: **ask for expected shortfall alongside VaR, and ask what distribution was assumed.** If the answer is "normal", the tail estimate is optimistic; if it is "historical", the estimate assumes the future resembles the sample period.

lesson.caption: What each measure is for and what it misses
rows: Skew and tails — treats gains and losses identically.
How bad a bad day is, at a chosen probability
Everything beyond the threshold; gameable by selling tail risk.
The average loss when the threshold is breached
Still depends on the assumed distribution.
The worst peak-to-trough fall that happened
The probability of a worse one — it is one observation.
What happens in a specified world

lesson.body:
**Volatility computed on smoothed marks.** Private assets' reported volatility is an artefact of quarterly estimation. Comparing it with a market-priced series is not a comparison.

**VaR from a quiet sample.** A historical VaR estimated over a calm period describes a calm period. The model is not wrong; the sample is.

**Treating a VaR limit as a risk framework.** It creates an incentive to hold positions with small daily moves and large rare losses, which is the opposite of the intent.

**Annualising volatility from short samples.** Scaling daily volatility by √252 assumes independence. Trending or mean-reverting series violate it, in opposite directions.

**Reporting drawdown from marks rather than realisable value.** A private portfolio's reported drawdown is the drawdown of its estimates. What it would have fetched is a different and larger number.

**One measure in isolation.** Volatility alone misses tails, VaR alone misses their size, drawdown alone misses probability. The set is the point.

**The risk that ends institutions is not the size of a loss. It is being made to act at the worst moment.**

Every expensive failure in modern markets has the same shape: a position that would have been fine if held, closed under duress. Long-Term Capital Management's convergence trades largely converged — after the fund was gone. The 2022 UK pension hedges were economically correct. Forced sellers in March 2020 sold to buyers who did very well.

So the useful risk question is not statistical. It is: **what could force us to act, and at what level?**

**[[covenant|Covenants]] and funding tests.** Thresholds with dates attached.

**Margin and collateral calls.** Cash demanded on a short cycle.

**Redemption terms.** Yours, and those of the funds you hold — a gate protects the fund and traps you.

**Governance.** A committee that will not tolerate a 25% drawdown has an effective stop-loss whether or not it has written one down. **That is a real constraint and it should be sized deliberately rather than discovered in a bad quarter.**

**Allocation limits.** A private markets cap breached by a public market fall, which forces action about assets that have not moved.

**None of these appear in volatility, VaR or drawdown.** They are the answer to "what actually goes wrong", and they are knowable in advance — which makes writing them down the highest-return risk exercise available.

**Ask for expected shortfall alongside VaR, and for the assumed distribution.** VaR without either is the least informative version of itself.

**Ask what sample period the risk estimates use, and whether it contains a crisis.** If not, they describe a regime rather than the strategy.

**Convert every drawdown into its recovery requirement.** "A 30% fall needs a 43% gain" lands with a committee in a way that "30% drawdown" does not.

**Write down every trigger that could force an action, with its level.** Covenants, margin, redemption terms, allocation limits, governance tolerance. That list is the real risk report.

**Check whether reported volatility rests on smoothed marks.** If it does, every risk-adjusted figure built on it is overstated, and the whole portfolio's risk is understated.

items: Volatility ignores shape, VaR ignores everything past its threshold, and drawdown is one observation with no probability attached. The set is the minimum honest report.
A 100m portfolio at 15% volatility has a 95% one-day VaR of 1.55m and an expected shortfall of about 1.95m — and the loss beyond the threshold is unbounded.
Drawdowns are asymmetric: 30% down needs 42.9% up, and 50% down needs 100%. Volatility treats the fall and an equal gain as the same information.

The risk that ends institutions is being forced to act. Covenants, margin, redemption terms, allocation limits and governance tolerance are the real risk report, and none appear in a statistical measure.

questions.stem: A portfolio has 15% annualised volatility. Using 252 trading days and a normal distribution, what is the 95% one-day VaR as a percentage of value? Two decimal places.
questions.inputHint: Daily volatility is annual ÷ √252; the 95% z-value is 1.645.
questions.explanation: On a 100m portfolio that is 1.55m. Note how much the answer depends on the normal assumption — real distributions have fatter tails, so the true frequency of worse days exceeds one in twenty.

questions.stem: A portfolio falls 30%. What percentage gain is needed to return to the previous peak? One decimal place.
questions.explanation: The asymmetry is why drawdowns dominate compound returns and why they feel worse than volatility suggests. At 50% down the requirement is a full double, which is a different kind of problem from a symmetric measure of variation.

questions.stem: What does a 95% one-day VaR of 1.55% tell you about the worst 5% of days?
choices: That losses on those days average 1.55%
Nothing at all — VaR is silent about the size of losses beyond its threshold
That losses on those days will not exceed 3.10%
That there is a 5% chance of losing everything
rationales: 1.55% is the threshold, not the average of the losses beyond it — that is expected shortfall, around 1.95% here.
Correct. VaR is a quantile. It marks a point in the distribution and says nothing about the shape past it, which is its central limitation.
No such bound exists; the tail is unbounded.
The 5% refers to the frequency of exceeding the threshold, not to total loss.
questions.explanation: This is why expected shortfall has replaced VaR in bank regulation, and why it is worth asking for. It is a strictly more informative number computed from the same data, and it is less flattering — which is largely why it appears less often in marketing material.

questions.stem: "Our VaR limit keeps portfolio risk controlled." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — a VaR limit rewards positions with small everyday moves and large rare losses, so it actively encourages selling tail risk
False — VaR limits are not used by real institutions
True — a binding VaR limit constrains risk by construction
False — because VaR cannot be computed for illiquid portfolios
rationales: Correct. Selling deep out-of-the-money options is the pure case: tiny daily moves, low VaR, catastrophic tail. The limit is satisfied and the risk is larger.
They are used extensively, which is exactly why the incentive matters.
It constrains the measured quantity, and the measured quantity is not the risk.
It is hard for illiquid portfolios and that is a separate limitation.
questions.explanation: The fix is a set rather than a single limit: VaR plus expected shortfall plus specified stress scenarios plus a list of forced-action triggers. Any single-number limit will be optimised against, and the optimisation is usually invisible until the tail arrives.

questions.stem: What do LTCM, the 2022 UK pension crisis and March 2020 forced sellers have in common?
choices: All involved positions that would have been acceptable if held, closed under duress by margin, collateral or governance pressure
All were caused by inadequate diversification
All were the result of models that were mathematically wrong
rationales: Correct. The economics were survivable and the funding was not. Being forced to act at the bottom converts a temporary loss into a permanent one.
Concentration contributed in some cases and is not the shared mechanism.
The models were mostly right about the economics and silent about liquidity and time.
questions.explanation: It reframes risk management as a liquidity and governance exercise rather than a statistical one. The most valuable half-hour available is writing down every trigger that could force an action and the level at which it fires.

questions.stem: A private portfolio reports a maximum drawdown of 8% while public equities fell 25% over the same period. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The private assets are genuinely eight times less risky
The drawdown is measured on quarterly manager estimates, which smooth and lag — the realisable drawdown was larger
Private assets have no correlation with public markets
rationales: Some resilience is real — no forced repricing, long holding periods — and a threefold difference is far larger than the economics support.
Correct. The reported drawdown is the drawdown of the estimates. What the assets would have fetched in a sale at the trough is a different and larger figure.
Possible in principle and rare, and it would be disclosed.
They are exposed to the same financing conditions and exit environment; the measured correlation is low partly because of the same smoothing.
questions.explanation: The question that tests it: what did assets actually sold during that period fetch relative to their prior marks? Secondary market pricing in the same window is the external check, and it is usually available.
